Maladaptive Strategies.value: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

vignette: Rajesh, a 46‑year‑old software engineer from the Bronx, returned home after a four‑year tour in Afghanistan. The day he was ambushed by a roadside bomb, a thunderous explosion of shrapnel filled the air, the acrid scent of burnt plastic clinging to his uniform, and the sudden roar of a motorcycle convoy that had been traveling in the distance. He was struck by a shard of glass that cut through his left thigh while his pants had slipped down to his knees in the heat of the moment. He woke that night with his clothes shredded, the metallic taste of blood, and the echo of gunfire still resonating in his ears. That single encounter set the stage for the sensory cues that would later trigger him, even in the quiet glow of his kitchen at night. The smell of gasoline from a passing delivery truck now flutters through Rajesh’s apartment and reminds him of the battlefield, while the mere suggestion of nudity—his own body exposed in a cramped, dusty tent—reminds him of that vulnerability he felt under enemy fire. Even the hum of a motorcycle on the highway, a sound that once meant safety, now sends a shiver through his spine. When these sensory triggers surface, Rajesh instinctively pulls the television remote away, avoids reading any news coverage about conflicts, and refuses to go outside even for a walk. His body’s alarm system has taken over: he feels perpetually on guard inside his own home, he avoids unfamiliar places because he cannot gauge the danger, and strangers approaching him in grocery lines give him the sense of imminent threat. The very act of hearing the sounds of gunfire replay in his head when he recalls the event; he hears the crunch of shrapnel, the hiss of the explosion, the distant thud of artillery. The memory of that day is not a wordless image—he cannot put it into words—but rather a looping film, its soundtrack replaying relentlessly in his mind. Because the triggers constantly activate his vigilance, his memories of the assault become sharper and more intrusive, reinforcing each other. When Rajesh tries to read or watch a documentary about war, the images trigger the same olfactory, visual, and auditory cues he has grown to dread. That avoidance of media feeds back into the persistent threat he feels, both at home and when he steps out. The fear that strangers might be hostile makes him skip the gym, a routine he had used to decompress from work. In turn, the avoidance of exercise removes a critical outlet for stress, leaving the memory of that fateful day unprocessed. The heightened threat perception also magnifies the triggers: the scent of gasoline is now a direct reminder of imminent danger, and the sound of a motorcycle’s engine becomes a potential alarm. Each of these reactions pulls him further into a loop of avoidance and threat that isolates him from colleagues, slows his coding at the software firm, and strains his marriage as his wife worries about his sudden withdrawal from everyday life. The memory of the battle is the raw material that keeps the cycle tight; every time he evades a trigger, the mind fills the silence with the haunting replay, which in turn drives him to shun even the simplest activities. Today, Rajesh sits at his kitchen table, the smell of burnt coffee grounds drifting past the open window. He has stopped going for morning jogs, declined lunch breaks with coworkers, and cut off weekend trips to the park. His mother’s phone call last week, asking why he hasn’t returned from the office, was the tipping point that finally brought him to the therapist’s office. He is terrified that one more trigger will send him spiraling back into that battlefield mind, that the memory will flood him so completely that he will lose control and perhaps harm himself or others. Yet, beneath that dread, there is a fragile hope that if he could untangle the web of triggers, memory, and threat, he might regain the quiet focus he once had on his screen, the laughter he once shared with his wife, and the peace of simply breathing in his own kitchen without fear.
